1.name: Jaeden Grimes
1.about: The projected No. 1 pick emerged as one of college basketball’s most dynamic freshman guards during his season at Washington. Grimes’ burst, powerful 196-pound frame and long 6'9" wingspan help him consistently create advantages downhill, while his polished midrange game gives him an answer when defenses cut off the rim. He pairs high-level scoring creation with legitimate lead-guard playmaking.

2.name: Rayan Ewane
2.about: Ewane has been one of the biggest risers in the draft, climbing from outside the preseason top five into the conversation at No. 2 overall. His rare combination of 7'0" size, a 7'6" wingspan, ball handling and advanced playmaking flourished against professional competition, establishing him as one of the class’s most unique high-upside prospects.

3.name: Ja'Corey Washington
3.about: The five-star and No. 1 recruit in the class validated the hype with an impressive freshman season at Kentucky. Washington's explosive athleticism, relentless motor and 7'3" wingspan made him a force around both rims, particularly as a shot blocker and offensive rebounder. Developing his perimeter skill set remains the biggest step toward reaching his considerable ceiling.

4.name: Caden Wilson
4.about: Entering the season as the projected No. 1 pick, Wilson ultimately settled into the top-five range after his freshman year at Kansas. At 6'5" and 203 pounds, he combines excellent guard size with deep range, advanced pull-up shooting and polished ball-screen scoring. His ability to manufacture perimeter offense remains one of the strongest skills in the class.

5.name: James Chonokolo
5.about: Chonokolo turned a strong sophomore season at Duke into a top-five draft profile, pairing a powerful interior game with legitimate floor-spacing ability. His 7'3" wingspan gives him disruptive defensive tools despite being undersized for a center, while his strength allows him to battle bigger opponents. His combination of shooting, post scoring and defensive versatility gives him multiple pathways to NBA impact.

6.name: Austin Almanza
6.about: UCLA brought Almanza over from Spain as one of its prized international recruits, and the freshman quickly justified the investment. His 7'5" wingspan, mobility and explosiveness made him an imposing presence around the rim, while his developing midrange game revealed intriguing offensive upside. His combination of production and physical tools has pushed him firmly into the top-10 conversation.

7.name: Jeremy Battle
7.about: One of the class’s most explosive downhill creators, Battle established himself as a dangerous attacking guard during his freshman season at North Carolina. He attacks the paint relentlessly, finishes through contact or above the rim and thrives when the game opens up in transition. His aggressive driving also creates opportunities for teammates, giving him legitimate upside as an attacking lead guard.

8.name: J'wuan Anderson
8.about: A prominent scorer dating back to high school, Anderson solidified himself as the best overall scorer in the draft during his freshman season at Missouri. His advanced handle, footwork and shot-making allow him to create from virtually anywhere, combining difficult pull-ups with deep range and isolation craft. Few prospects in the class possess his natural ability to manufacture offense.

9.name: Austyn Oliver
9.about: Once a four-star recruit, Oliver made a significant jump during his sophomore season at Ohio State and developed into one of the biggest risers in the class. His deep shooting range and pull-up ability have become legitimate weapons, while improved command with the ball allows him to create efficiently for himself and consistently generate opportunities for teammates.

10.name: Willie Broyles
10.about: An outstanding freshman season at North Carolina established Broyles as the best defender in the class, combining elite athleticism, strength and lateral quickness to legitimately guard across positions. His disruptive defense and relentless motor have driven his rise into the top-10 conversation. Offensive development, particularly as a shooter, will determine just how high his ceiling extends.

11.name: Marc-André Marin
11.about: Once viewed as a potential top-five pick, Marin saw his stock cool during the season but remains firmly in the lottery conversation. His length, mobility and defensive instincts continue to stand out against professional competition, particularly around the rim. Questions about his offensive ceiling and inconsistent perimeter shooting contributed to his slide.

12.name: Declan Richardson
12.about: One of the more well-rounded international wings in the class, Richardson brings legitimate two-way value with his size, shooting and defensive instincts. He spaces the floor effectively, generates steals with active hands and contributes strongly on the glass for his position, giving him several ways to impact games without needing heavy offensive usage.

13.name: Adnan Kovačević
13.about: After spending his freshman year as a role player off Michigan State’s bench, Kovačević transferred to Kansas and exploded into a lottery prospect. His enormous 7'3" frame and 7'9" wingspan transformed the paint defensively, while increased minutes showcased his rebounding and interior finishing. Limited mobility remains the primary concern surrounding his NBA translation.

14.name: Trey Fletcher II
14.about: Three seasons at Virginia have seen Fletcher steadily expand his game, improving his production and skill set each year. His junior breakout showcased explosive finishing, defensive versatility and a more dependable perimeter jumper. That consistent development has strengthened his first-round case, with scouts betting that his upward trajectory can continue at the next level.

15.name: Nailal Weyalloba
15.about: Weyalloba established himself as one of the class’s most physically dominant big men, bringing elite explosiveness, strength and length to Kentucky’s frontcourt. He overwhelms the rim as a lob threat and generates defensive plays with his 7'5" wingspan. His offensive game remains extremely limited outside the paint, but his athletic tools give him considerable two-way upside.

16.name: Trey Magana
16.about: Entering the season projected as a top-10 pick, Magana slipped down the board as defensive concerns emerged during his sophomore campaign. His explosive finishing, strength and activity around the rim remain highly appealing, but inconsistent positioning and difficulty defending in space raised questions about his NBA role. His physical tools still give him considerable upside.

17.name: Joe Ames
17.about: Heavy minutes were a constant throughout Ames’ four years at Iowa, where he became the steady hand behind the offense and established himself as an iron man. His experience shows in his patient pick-and-roll reads, confident pull-up shooting and ability to control tempo. His consistent availability and production have made him one of the most seasoned and dependable guards in the class.

18.name: Yitzhak Mizrah
18.about: Meaningful minutes against professional competition helped Mizrah establish himself as a legitimate first-round prospect with Hapoel Tel Aviv. The left-handed guard combines composed playmaking with disruptive point-of-attack defense, consistently anticipating passing lanes and creating turnovers. His experience operating against older competition gives him a mature two-way foundation entering the NBA.

19.name: Raylan Williams
19.about: Williams showcased a polished scoring arsenal during his freshman season at Duke, particularly when operating in the middle of the floor. His size allows him to shoot over smaller guards, while his footwork and touch make him comfortable creating pull-ups and difficult midrange looks. His combination of size and shot-making gives him intriguing upside as a secondary scorer at the next level.

20.name: Oskaras Vaškys
20.about: Controlling Seton Hall’s offense with patience and creativity, Vaškys developed into one of the more productive lead guards in college basketball. He excels navigating ball screens, creating pull-ups in the midrange and using changes of pace to manipulate defenders before finding teammates. His combination of scoring craft and high-level distribution gives him a polished offensive profile.

21.name: Frank Horn IV
21.about: An immediate jolt of athleticism in USC’s backcourt, Horn used his burst and aggressive mentality to consistently get downhill. Though undersized at 6'2", his 6'7" wingspan helps compensate, giving him extra reach as a finisher and defender. He excels in transition and has shown enough playmaking flashes to offer intriguing developmental upside at point guard.

22.name: Kemal Jones
22.about: After transferring from Washington following his freshman season, former five-star recruit Jones quickly grew into a larger offensive role at Wisconsin. Still only 19, he thrives in the middle of the floor with his change of pace, pull-up touch and creative passing. His youth and developing command as a lead guard leave plenty of room for continued growth.

23.name: Treyton Hernandez
23.about: A valuable two-way role emerged for Hernandez during his junior season at Villanova, pairing reliable perimeter shooting with intelligent team defense. His ability to space the floor gives him a clear offensive role, while his strength and positioning help compensate for modest size and athleticism. His physical limitations remain the biggest concern projecting him to the NBA.

24.name: Bilal Khelifi
24.about: Khelifi has emerged as an intriguing young wing in France, using his 7'1" wingspan and athleticism to make an impact on both ends despite playing a relatively modest offensive role. He excels attacking open space, finishing above the rim and using his length defensively, giving him a projectable two-way foundation at just 19 years old.

25.name: Darrell Anderson Jr.
25.about: Anderson put together an impressive freshman season at Stanford, pairing soft interior touch with legitimate two-way value. His mobility and 7'3" wingspan allow him to protect the rim, cover ground defensively and handle switches better than many young bigs. He remains limited as a shooter, but his finishing and defensive versatility provide a strong developmental foundation.

26.name: Aziel Bailey
26.about: Few players in the class can match Bailey’s ability to manufacture offense off the dribble. The undersized lefty emerged as one of the class’s most dangerous scorers, combining advanced pull-up shooting, tough shot-making and sharp changes of pace. His scoring talent is undeniable, though his size creates questions about finishing and defensive versatility at the next level.

27.name: Colt Bodnar
27.about: Bodnar developed into one of college basketball’s most dependable interior anchors during his senior season, using his massive 7'7" wingspan to control the paint and dominate the defensive glass. He compensates for limited athleticism with positioning and timing, while flashes of shooting touch add intrigue. His lack of mobility remains the biggest concern for NBA defenses.

28.name: Ajani Martin
28.about: After playing a small role on a stacked Michigan team as a freshman, Martin grew into his own with expanded opportunities this season. His strength, long arms and creative finishing helped him become a reliable downhill threat, while increased on-ball responsibility revealed more of his scoring potential. Improving his jumper remains the key to rounding out his offensive game.

29.name: Marcel Wilson
29.about: After two seasons at St. John’s, Wilson transferred to a stacked North Carolina team and carved out an important role without needing to dominate the ball. His physical finishing, cutting and improved perimeter shooting allowed him to thrive alongside higher-usage talent, strengthening his projection as an adaptable NBA role player.

30.name: Genaro Ibáñez
30.about: Ibáñez has developed into a versatile offensive initiator for Obras Sanitarias, using his 6'7" frame to see over defenses and create for himself or teammates. His pull-up shooting and advanced pick-and-roll feel allow him to function as a secondary ball handler, with his combination of shot-making, passing and positional size driving his NBA intrigue.

31.name: Kyle Martell
31.about: Martell capped his senior season at St. John’s as one of the most productive perimeter scorers in college basketball. His movement shooting, deep range and quick release powered a heavy scoring workload, while his pull-up game gave him another weapon against aggressive closeouts. His shooting versatility remains the clear foundation of his NBA projection.

32.name: Jahari Johnson
32.about: Johnson carved out an impactful two-way role at Texas by leaning into his exceptional strength and athleticism. The powerful 225-pound wing attacks gaps aggressively, finishes through contact and brings considerable energy defensively. His improved perimeter shooting has rounded out his game, giving him a complementary skill set that translates well to an NBA role.

33.name: Troy Reeves Jr.
33.about: Reeves entered his freshman season projected as a top-10 pick, but gradually slipped down the board despite showcasing his polished perimeter scoring at Oklahoma. His shooting, change of pace and ability to create jumpers remain attractive NBA skills, though questions surrounding his athletic ceiling and defensive impact have pushed him toward the late-first-round conversation.

34.name: Johnathan Mays
34.about: An aggressive downhill approach allowed Mays to flash considerable upside during his freshman season at Oklahoma State. He attacks gaps decisively, finishes explosively when given a runway and has shown flashes of playmaking off penetration. His physical tools and attacking mentality give him an appealing developmental foundation in the backcourt.

35.name: Julien Michel
35.about: Michel handled a meaningful role for Monaco, providing consistent scoring and floor spacing against experienced professional competition. At 6'8", he combines shooting touch with smart off-ball movement and enough finishing ability to capitalize inside. His productive minutes on a talented Monaco roster have strengthened his case as a potential NBA rotation forward.

36.name: Mike Farrrow
36.about: An aggressive attacking style powered Farrrow’s productive junior season at Providence. Despite standing just 6'1", his exceptional 6'7" wingspan helps him play larger around the basket, where he uses quickness, creativity and vertical pop to finish. He consistently pushes the pace and creates paint touches, giving him a clear identity as a change-of-pace guard.

37.name: Darrius Melton
37.about: Melton spent his freshman season in a bench role behind Adnan Kovačević, but made a strong impression whenever his number was called. His powerful 258-pound frame, explosive leaping and 7'3" wingspan produced flashes of dominant interior play in limited minutes. His physical upside is intriguing, though his offensive skill set remains raw.

38.name: Jalen Shelton
38.about: Shelton developed into one of the more skilled offensive bigs in college basketball, combining polished post footwork and soft midrange touch with impressive passing instincts. Auburn regularly ran offense through him in the half court, where he punished double teams and found cutters. Limited athleticism and perimeter mobility remain his biggest NBA concerns.

39.name: Mario Jurić
39.about: Jurić has built his offensive game around patience and craft, consistently finding openings inside the arc against professional competition. The 6'5" lefty uses changes of pace, footwork and soft touch to create in the midrange while flashing secondary playmaking ability. His skill level is intriguing, though average athleticism limits his margin for error against NBA defenders.

40.name: Kevin Vaughn
40.about: Intriguing two-way flashes highlighted Vaughn's freshman season at Florida State, where he used his strength and 7'0" wingspan to defend multiple positions and finish forcefully around the basket. His defensive tools provide a strong foundation, but an inconsistent jumper and limited creation kept his offensive role relatively simple and his draft stock in second-round territory.

41.name: Ian Petty
41.about: Petty’s physical style stood out throughout his junior season at Xavier, where he consistently used his powerful frame and explosiveness to pressure defenses. He attacks the paint aggressively, absorbs contact and can defend bigger perimeter players despite standing just 6'3". His unusual dimensions are intriguing, but improving his jumper will be crucial to his NBA fit.

42.name: Dale Adams Jr
42.about: Defense provided Adams with his pathway to immediate minutes at Texas, where his excellent length and instincts regularly disrupted opposing guards at the point of attack. His 6'10" wingspan allows him to switch across multiple perimeter positions, generate deflections and recover when beaten. Offensively, he showed encouraging flashes as a spot-up shooter and secondary ball handler.

43.name: Michel Charbonnier
43.about: Charbonnier earned rotational minutes against professional competition with Paris, flashing intriguing defensive ability despite a limited statistical role. His mobility and timing give him potential as a versatile interior defender, while his developing jumper offers some long-term offensive upside. He remains a projection pick whose NBA value will depend heavily on continued offensive development.

44.name: Aboubacar Walker
44.about: Walker’s junior season at Georgetown highlighted the defensive versatility that makes him an intriguing NBA prospect. At 6'8" with a 7'2" wingspan and impressive athleticism, he covers considerable ground, disrupts passing lanes and attacks the rim in transition. His physical profile gives him multiple pathways toward becoming a valuable two-way forward.

45.name: Donnie Moore
45.about: Moore became a dependable source of perimeter offense for Tennessee, using his shooting instincts and polished footwork to find opportunities both on and off the ball. The left-handed junior is comfortable relocating for threes or creating space for pull-ups, though limited burst makes it difficult for him to consistently pressure the rim against athletic defenders.

46.name: Terry Saunders
46.about: Few players in the class offer Saunders’ level of immediate shooting reliability. The 23-year-old senior stretches defenses with deep range, a quick release and intelligent movement away from the ball, while his relentless hustle helps him contribute beyond his scoring. His age limits his upside, but his shooting and high-effort play give him a clear NBA role.

47.name: Kameron Steward
47.about: By his senior season at Indiana, Steward had developed into a dependable defensive big, using his 7'3" wingspan and timing to consistently challenge shots around the basket. He provides value as a rim runner and active finisher offensively, but his thin frame, limited shooting and modest athleticism create questions about how his game translates to the NBA.

48.name: Jason Clark Jr.
48.about: After transferring from Pittsburgh to Texas, Clark settled into a valuable complementary role during his senior season. He made his impact without needing touches, producing as a cutter, offensive rebounder and transition finisher while bringing defensive activity across the frontcourt. His age, undersized frame and limited creation cap his upside, but his versatility gives him a potential NBA role.

49.name: Josh Landon
49.about: Landon developed into a productive two-way wing during his junior season at Wake Forest, using his length and open-floor ability to consistently create pressure at the rim. He thrives as a cutter and transition finisher while showing enough perimeter touch to keep defenses honest, giving him a useful complementary offensive profile.

50.name: William Renner
50.about: A productive senior season at Kansas State has Renner entering the draft as a projected second-round pick. His shooting touch, footwork and offensive feel give him a potential role as a floor-spacing big, but limited athleticism and length restrict his defensive versatility. Teams will be weighing his polished offensive skill against questions about his NBA defensive fit.

51.name: P.J. Fuller
51.about: A former five-star recruit who entered Oregon with significant expectations, Fuller gradually slid down draft boards during his freshman season. His shooting touch and offensive skill remain intriguing, but poor athleticism, limited defensive impact and an awkward positional fit exposed concerns against higher-level competition. His offensive upside keeps him firmly in the second-round mix.

52.name: Qua'sean Clark
52.about: After spending his freshman season at Louisville, Clark transferred to Oklahoma and settled into a complementary role as a sophomore. His straight-line driving, cutting and transition play allowed him to contribute without requiring many touches, while his length and developing perimeter shot give him a potential pathway toward an NBA role.

53.name: Dereece Hayes
53.about: Hayes emerged as an energetic rotation forward during his sophomore season at Arkansas, using his explosive athleticism and strong frame to make an impact around the basket. He excels as a cutter, transition finisher and offensive rebounder, while flashes of perimeter shooting give him additional upside as a versatile complementary forward.

54.name: Tre Short
54.about: Short put together a solid freshman season at Memphis, but being 20 years old limits some of the developmental appeal typically attached to a first-year prospect. His 6'8" frame, cutting, straight-line driving and developing jumper give him useful complementary tools, though scouts will want to see a more polished all-around game from an older freshman.

55.name: Ishaq Williams
55.about: Power, defensive intensity and relentless rim pressure became the foundation of Williams’ senior season at Washington State. His strong frame and long arms allow him to overwhelm smaller guards, absorb contact on drives and defend multiple backcourt matchups. He brings a physical edge on both ends, giving him a distinct identity despite an offensive game that remains heavily centered around attacking the paint.

56.name: Josh Serna
56.about: Serna established himself as a defensive specialist during his junior season at UCF, using his mobility and 7'3" wingspan to switch comfortably onto smaller players. Still only 20 despite three college seasons, he offers more developmental runway than the typical junior prospect. His defensive versatility is intriguing, but his limited offensive game remains the major obstacle.

57.name: Tyler Richards
57.about: A transfer from Tennessee, Richards found a more productive role at Alabama and established himself as an aggressive downhill guard. He does his best work attacking closeouts, getting into the paint and running the floor, while showing flashes as a secondary playmaker. His combination of length and slashing gives him developmental appeal as a versatile reserve guard.

58.name: Amani Ellis
58.about: After transferring from Missouri, Ellis found a complementary role at Kansas by bringing physicality and defensive energy to the perimeter. His 6'10" wingspan allows him to play bigger than his listed height, while his downhill mentality creates opportunities around the basket. Developing a more dependable jumper remains important to expanding his offensive value.

59.name: Dequinn Robertson
59.about: After developing into a dependable two-way contributor at Maryland, Robertson enters the draft near the end of the second-round picture. His athleticism, length and cutting allow him to impact games without needing touches, while his defensive versatility offers additional value. An unreliable jumper remains the biggest obstacle to securing a consistent NBA role.

60.name: Iago Barcellos
60.about: A steady role with Pinheiros has helped Barcellos enter the draft as a borderline second-round prospect. His midrange touch, footwork and defensive awareness give him a polished foundation, but average athleticism and limited length restrict his upside. Expanding his three-point range could be crucial to establishing a viable NBA role.

61.name: Bo Riley
61.about: A dependable veteran presence throughout his Kentucky career, Riley carved out his value through shooting and disruptive perimeter defense. He plays with constant activity away from the ball, pressures opposing handlers and looks to turn mistakes into transition opportunities. Offensively, his quick release and comfort shooting off movement give him a pathway toward a specialist role.

62.name: Johnny Lowry
62.about: Lowry was a productive interior presence for Wisconsin as a senior, using his 256-pound frame, strength and polished post game to manufacture offense around the basket. He also consistently created second-chance opportunities on the glass. At just 6'8" with limited length and athleticism, however, his traditional interior style creates significant questions about his NBA translation.

63.name: Matt Bowden
63.about: A productive junior campaign at Loyola Maryland established Bowden as a skilled stretch forward with legitimate shooting touch. His ability to space the floor has earned NBA interest, but severe athletic limitations, modest length and defensive concerns leave him just outside the 60-pick draft range and fighting for a two-way opportunity.

64.name: Tyler John
64.about: John carved out a productive interior role at Cincinnati through physicality, screening and hard rim runs. He does most of his offensive damage as a finisher rather than a creator, while competing on the glass and defensively inside. At 6'8" with limited explosiveness and virtually no perimeter game, his NBA role is difficult to project.

65.name: Samir Jones
65.about: Jones served as a veteran role player on a stacked North Carolina team, providing dependable shooting and perimeter defense without requiring many touches. His ability to space the floor, make quick decisions and defend within a team structure helped him contribute alongside more talented scorers, though his limited athletic upside caps his NBA ceiling.

66.name: Max Jenkins
66.about: A four-year player at Virginia, Jenkins gradually developed into a reliable veteran scorer and floor spacer. His experience shows in his off-ball movement, shot preparation and understanding of how to operate within a structured offense. While his age and limited burst restrict his upside, his shooting gives him a clear pathway toward an NBA role.

67.name: Colton Mills
67.about: After spending much of his college career as a backup, Mills earned Purdue’s starting center job as a senior and made the most of the opportunity. He provided steady interior scoring, rebounding and physicality while flashing impressive athleticism for his size. The breakout improved his draft outlook, though his limited shooting and defensive versatility still cloud his NBA fit.

68.name: Tony Flowers
68.about: A crafty veteran scorer, Flowers capped his Miami career by consistently using changes of pace and a tight handle to create space on the perimeter. He is comfortable navigating ball screens, getting defenders off balance and converting pull-ups when given room. His experience and ability to provide shooting and secondary creation give him a potential reserve role at the next level.

69.name: Joe Wiley
69.about: Projected to go undrafted, Wiley remains an intriguing skill-based guard after a productive senior season at BYU. His deep shooting range, controlled handle and pick-and-roll passing give him offensive utility, but limited size and athleticism create significant questions defensively. His shooting and decision-making could still earn him an opportunity as a developmental guard.

70.name: Rajko Radosavljević
70.about: Consistent rotation minutes for Partizan allowed Radosavljević to hold his own against professional competition with his strength, scoring touch and polished midrange game. He produced efficiently without commanding a major offensive role, but questions surrounding his tweener size, defensive mobility and perimeter shooting have kept him outside the projected 60 picks despite his experience.

71.name: Will Krajisnik
71.about: Krajisnik provided Duke with veteran stability on the wing, making his biggest impact as a floor spacer and disciplined team defender. He shoots confidently off the catch, understands how to relocate around higher-usage teammates and rarely needs the ball to contribute. His experience, shooting and understanding of his role give him a chance to compete for minutes despite a modest physical ceiling.

72.name: Weston Ellison
72.about: Ellison developed into a steady perimeter scorer during his senior season at Virginia Tech, relying on craft and shooting touch rather than athleticism. At 6'5", he can operate comfortably off screens or create pull-ups against softer coverage, while also handling occasional secondary playmaking duties. His ability to generate offense from the perimeter remains his strongest selling point as he looks to carve out a professional role.

73.name: Rodney Thompson
73.about: Thompson brings an unconventional combination of strength, shooting touch and passing feel from the wing. At 220 pounds, he uses his sturdy frame to protect the ball and create passing angles, while remaining capable of spacing the floor off the catch. His lack of burst and undersized wing dimensions create questions about how effectively his game translates defensively.

74.name: Qw'uan Morrison
74.about: Following three seasons at Alabama, Morrison transferred to Creighton and carved out a productive senior role through physicality, rebounding and relentless interior work. His strength made him effective on the glass and around the basket, but limited shooting and perimeter skill leave him projected outside the 60 picks despite his high-major experience.

75.name: Corey Rizzo
75.about: A highly productive senior season at Weber State showcased Rizzo's shooting touch, positioning and offensive feel as a stretch big. His ability to space the floor gives him a potential specialist pathway, but at 23 with poor athleticism, limited length and defensive concerns, he enters the process as a likely undrafted prospect.
